title: profiling-tooling-and-scripts-runbook-v6
content:
Purpose:
This runbook collects the canonical tooling, scripts, CI behavior, and troubleshooting steps we use for serving-runtime performance investigations. It covers perf CI jobs, flamegraphs for CPU & Python, GPU trace collection, tracing integration, and where artifacts are stored for analysis and alerts.

Scope and intent:
- Day-to-day: quick repro profiling, flamegraphs to find hot paths, capture GPU timelines for kernel-level regressions.
- CI: automated nightly + PR perf checks that generate artifacts and fail on regressions beyond thresholds.
- Runbook: steps to triage common performance regressions and collect artifacts for postmortems.

Key tools we use (summary):
- perf (Linux) + FlameGraph scripts (Brendan Gregg) for native/C++ stacks.
- py-spy for Python sampling flamegraphs (safe in production).
- nsys (Nsight Systems) / ncu (Nsight Compute) for GPU timelines and kernel metrics.
- eBPF/bcc/bpftrace snippets for kernel/IO hotspots and sched stats.
- OpenTelemetry + Jaeger/Zipkin for distributed traces.
- Prometheus/Grafana for metrics; traces and spans linked from dashboards.
- Artifacts storage: s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/ (CI) and temporary local /tmp/perf-uploads.

Perf CI job (high level):
- Pipeline name: ci/redwood/perf-bench
- Triggers: nightly on main branch; on-demand for release branches; optional PR gating for large PRs (configurable).
- Steps:
  1) Checkout commit and build with perf flags (DEBUG=false, PERF_BUILD=true).
  2) Spin test harness VMs/containers (exact config from pipelines/perf/bench-config.yml).
  3) Warmup run (configurable warmup seconds to populate KV cache and JIT warm paths).
  4) Run scenarios (microbenchmarks + end-to-end benchmark traces).
  5) Collect artifacts: latency/throughput histograms (JSON), cpu flamegraphs, python flamegraphs, nsys timeline exports (.qdrep/.nsys-rep), kernel traces if present.
  6) Upload artifacts to s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/<commit>/<date>/ and publish a summary report with baseline comparisons.
  7) Fail the job when regression rules are hit (see thresholds below).

Perf CI thresholds (current defaults):
- 95th latency increase > 5% (relative) => FAIL
- 50th latency increase > 8% => WARN (and leave artifact)
- Throughput drop > 3% => FAIL
- Regression on memory usage (RSS) > 10% => FAIL
These thresholds live in pipelines/perf/regression-rules.yml and are tuned by eng-serving-runtime.

How to run a local perf capture (dev machine or debug box):
1) Native/C++ flamegraph (Linux):
   - build with debug symbols: make BUILD_TYPE=relwithdebinfo
   - warm the server for your scenario (same warmup as CI)
   - perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60
   - perf script > out.perf
   - ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl out.perf > out.folded
   - ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
   Notes: if the server runs in container, use --host or run perf inside the container with CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

2) Python flamegraph (py-spy):
   - py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <pid> --duration 60 --rate 100
   - or run under py-spy: py-spy top -- python -m server.main --args
   Important: py-spy is safe in prod and does not require ptrace attach flags if the binary is the same user.

3) GPU timeline (Nsight Systems):
   - nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,cudnn,nvtx -- python ./benchmark_client.py --target <url>
   - nsys export --force --output /tmp/trace.html /tmp/trace.qdrep  (open in browser)
   - For kernel metrics per-kernel: ncu -o /tmp/kernels --target-processes all --set full ./server_binary [args]
   Notes: nsys is our primary timeline tool; nvprof is deprecated on recent drivers.

4) Collecting stacks + GPU counters for single request slow path:
   - reproduce a slow request with low concurrency, then capture nsys + perf simultaneously:
     perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30 &
     nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,nvtx -- python reproduce_slow_request.py
   - Upload both artifacts and link in the incident.

Scripts and locations (common):
- repo: serving-runtime/scripts/perf/run_perf_ci.sh  (wrapper to run a single scenario locally or in CI)
- repo: serving-runtime/scripts/perf/generate_flame.sh  (helper that runs perf/py-spy and produces flame.svg)
- repo: serving-runtime/scripts/perf/collect_nsys.sh
- pipelines: .pipelines/perf-bench.yml  (CI config, scenarios, and regression rules)
- FlameGraph tools are vendored under tooling/FlameGraph/ (stackcollapse-perf.pl, flamegraph.pl)

Artifact naming conventions:
- <commit>-<scenario>-<hostname>-<timestamp>-<type> (e.g., 9a1b2c3b-small_batch-gpu-2026-02-19-flame.svg)
- Each CI run writes a metadata.json alongside artifacts with: commit, git-ref, branch, scenario, machine-type, docker image, and perf stats.

Comparison & baselines:
- The CI job compares current stats to the baseline commit stored as baseline/<scenario>.json in s3. Baselines are rotated weekly.
- For flamegraphs we keep both current and baseline flame.svg files and provide a quick visual diff link in the generated HTML report (side-by-side).

Tracing and spans (distributed):
- We instrument hot code paths with OpenTelemetry spans. Use environment flags to enable verbose span export in staging: OTEL_EXPORTER=jaeger OTEL_AGENT_HOST=jaeger.internal
- When investigating a request tail latency, capture the trace id and retrieve spans from Jaeger UI; link that trace id to the CI artifacts.

Common investigation checklist (step-by-step):
1) Verify the regression claim: check CI perf JSON for scenario, confirm percent changes and absolute deltas for 50/95/99 latency and throughput.
2) Reproduce locally with same scenario (warmup, input shape, batch size).
3) Capture CPU flamegraph and Python flamegraph concurrently (perf + py-spy).
4) Capture GPU timeline with nsys if kernels or GPU time suspect.
5) Check system metrics: CPU steal, load, IRQ, NIC drops, memory pressure (dmesg), and ulimit.
6) If NVidia GPU: check driver version, persistence mode and MIG partitioning differences between baseline and regression hosts.
7) Search for recent PRs that touched kernels, dispatcher, batching, KV cache, or compilation/kernels selection (use git blame and linked PRs).
8) If root cause unclear, collect strace on a short repro to see syscalls and blocking IO.
9) Attach artifacts and assign to owner with a short hypothesis and next steps.

Triage patterns and likely causes (examples):
- Increased CPU overhead in request parsing => big C++ string copies or Python layer regressions. Look for large stacks in perf flame.
- GPU kernel slowdown => new kernel launch parameters or changed input shapes causing different code path; analyze nsys timeline and ncu metrics.
- Higher tail latency under load => batching policy change or lock contention; use eBPF sched latency and perf to find contended locks.
- Memory growth/regression => leak in KV cache or per-request allocation; check heaptrack/valgrind or google-perftools heap profiler.

Quick troubleshooting commands (copyable):
- perf for pid: perf record -F 99 -p $(pidof server) -g -- sleep 60
- produce folded: perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > /tmp/out.folded
- make flame: ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl /tmp/out.folded > /tmp/flame.svg
- py-spy: py-spy record -o /tmp/pyflame.svg --pid <pid> --duration 60
- nsys timeline: nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,nvtx -- python reproduce.py
- upload artifacts: aws s3 cp /tmp/flame.svg s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/<commit>/<date>/ --acl private

Notes / gotchas:
- perf requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN on some kernels or running as root; in containers prefer running the capture on the host or grant appropriate capabilities.
- py-spy might not attach across user boundaries; run as same user.
- nsys profiles change timing behavior (overhead) — use low-overhead sampling and correlate with plain production metrics.
- Flamegraphs are sampling-based; a cold JIT or one-off IO will appear differently than wall-clock traces.

Where to file follow-ups and linking conventions:
- If CI fails, create a Jira under component=serving-runtime/perf with title prefixed [perf-regression] and include commit, scenario, artifacts s3 link, and preliminary hypothesis. Example ticket: SERV-421.
- Include references to relevant PRs and the nightly perf job id.

References and related runbooks:
- existing docs: profiling-tooling-and-scripts-runbook.json (v1..v5) in this directory (look for historical notes and older workflows)
- Confluence: https://confluence.internal/redwood/serving-runtime/perf-runbook
- GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+label%3Aperf

If you are new to this runbook and need help: ping #eng-serving-runtime in Slack and tag @Aisha for onboarding walkthroughs for the tooling and CI flows.
